The study of how hormone systems and the central nervous system are linked in structure and function, and how behavior shapes and is shaped by both.
A test in which a drug or hormone is given to perturb an endocrine axis in a standard way; more reliable than a single baseline sample because most hormones are released in pulses.
Lasting effects of hormones, such as gonadal steroids, on brain structure and function during critical periods of development.
Acute, reversible effects of current hormone levels on brain function, such as higher estrogen briefly raising sensitivity to serotonin.
A test of HPA axis feedback; failure to suppress cortisol after dexamethasone is reported in depression but is not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose it.
A deficiency of the enzyme 21-hydroxylase that exposes the person to high adrenal androgens before and after birth.
DHEA; with its sulfate the most abundant circulating steroid, an adrenal androgen released in response to ACTH and also made in the brain as a neurosteroid.
The prepubertal start of adrenal DHEA-S production.
A proposed index of how well a person is buffered against the harmful effects of stress; higher ratios go with greater fear-potentiated startle.
Feedback of a pituitary hormone on the hypothalamus, as when prolactin limits its own release.
A soluble signaling protein released by immune cells and microglia that carries messages between immune cells and acts on the brain.
Suppression of an immune response by a conditioned stimulus, first shown when saccharin paired with cyclophosphamide later lowered antibody responses when given alone.
A cytokine-driven cluster of dysphoria, anhedonia, fatigue, social withdrawal, poor appetite, altered sleep, heightened pain and cognitive slowing seen with infection or chronic stress.
An animal model in which an immune challenge to the pregnant mother, acting through interleukin 6, changes the behavior and gene transcription of the offspring.
Retroviral sequences carried in every human genome that can alter the transcription of host genes; proposed as one route to schizophrenia.
Proteins such as C-reactive protein and complement that rise with inflammation; found with amyloid plaques in Alzheimer disease.
